slides.narration: A porter drags a trunk along a platform, and a stone is lifted to a roof. In both, a force acts through a distance. In this part we measure that effort as work, link it to the kinetic energy a body gains, and meet stored energy in a raised stone and a stretched spring.

slides.heading: What is work?
slides.body_md: In physics, **work** is done when a force moves the body it acts on. Only the part of the force **along the displacement** counts.
bullets: Work is a **scalar**: it has a sign but no direction.
SI unit: the **joule** (J). $1$ J is the work of a force of $1$ N when the body moves $1$ m along the force, so $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{N m}$.
Dimensions $[\text{M}\,\text{L}^{2}\,\text{T}^{-2}]$. In the CGS system the unit is the **erg**, and $1\ \text{J} = 10^{7}$ erg.
Pushing hard against a wall that does not move does no work.

rows: 1 J = 1 N m: the work of a force of 1 N moving its point of application 1 m along the force
The same as energy; work is a scalar

slides.narration: In physics, work is done only when a force moves the body it acts on, and only the part of the force along the displacement counts. Work is a scalar, so it has a sign but no direction. Its unit is the joule, which is one newton metre. In the smaller C G S system the unit is the erg, and one joule is ten million ergs. Pushing a wall that does not move does no work.

slides.heading: Work done by a constant force
slides.body_md: A constant force $\vec F$ acts on a body whose displacement is $\vec S$, with angle $\theta$ between them. The work is the **scalar (dot) product**:
bullets: $F\cos\theta$ is the component of the force along the displacement; $F\sin\theta$ is perpendicular to it and does **no** work.
In the figure a strap pulls a trolley with $90$ N at $35^\circ$ above the track through $12$ m: $W = 73.7 \times 12 = 884.7$ J.
$S$ is the **displacement** of the body, not the length of the path, and $F$ must stay constant in size and direction.

slides.narration: When a constant force makes an angle theta with the displacement, the work done is the force times the displacement times the cosine of theta. This is the scalar product of the two vectors. The part of the force across the displacement does no work. In the figure the pull is ninety newtons at thirty five degrees through twelve metres, so the work is eight hundred and eighty five joules.

slides.heading: Positive, zero and negative work
slides.body_md: The sign of $W = FS\cos\theta$ is the sign of $\cos\theta$.
bullets: **Positive** ($0^\circ \le \theta < 90^\circ$): the force has a component along the motion and the body **gains** energy.
**Zero** ($\theta = 90^\circ$, or no displacement): the force is perpendicular to the motion, as for the weight of a trunk carried along a level platform.
**Negative** ($90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$): the force opposes the motion, as friction or the brakes do; the body **loses** energy.

slides.narration: The sign of the work follows the sign of the cosine of the angle. If the force has a component along the motion, the work is positive and the body gains energy. If the force is perpendicular to the motion, as the weight of a trunk carried along a level platform, the work is zero. If the force opposes the motion, as friction does, the work is negative and the body loses energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: pulling a trolley
slides.body_md: A porter pulls a luggage trolley through $12$ m along a level platform with a strap that exerts a constant force of $90$ N at $35^\circ$ above the horizontal. Find the work done by (i) the strap, (ii) the weight and the normal reaction of the platform.
bullets: (i) $W = FS\cos\theta = 90 \times 12 \times \cos 35^\circ = 90 \times 12 \times 0.8192 = 884.7$ J.
(ii) Weight and normal reaction are vertical, perpendicular to the displacement: $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, so each does **zero** work.
Had the strap been horizontal the work would be $90 \times 12 = 1080$ J: tilting the strap wastes a part of the pull.

slides.heading: Work by a variable force: area under the F–S graph
slides.body_md: When the force changes along the path, divide the displacement into thin strips $\Delta S$. In each strip $F$ is nearly constant, so the work is $\Delta W = F\,\Delta S$, the **area of the strip**. Adding all the strips:
bullets: **Work = area under the force–displacement graph** between the two limits.
For a constant force the area is a rectangle, $W = FS$.
Area **below** the S-axis (force opposing the displacement) counts as **negative** work.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a handcart on a rough track
slides.body_md: The graph shows the force exerted along the track on a loaded handcart as it is pushed through $9$ m. Find the work done.
bullets: From $0$ to $2$ m the force rises from $0$ to $30$ N: a triangle, $\tfrac12 \times 2 \times 30 = 30$ J.
From $2$ m to $6$ m it stays at $30$ N: a rectangle, $4 \times 30 = 120$ J.
From $6$ m to $9$ m it falls from $30$ N to $10$ N: a trapezium, $\tfrac12 (30 + 10) \times 3 = 60$ J.

slides.heading: Kinetic energy
slides.body_md: The **kinetic energy** of a body of mass $m$ moving with speed $v$ is the energy it has because of its motion:
bullets: It is a **scalar** and never negative; its unit is the joule.
It depends on the **square** of the speed: doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.
In terms of momentum $p = mv$: $K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}$, so for equal momenta the lighter body has the larger kinetic energy.

rows: Same cyclist at double the speed

visual.alt: Table of the kinetic energy of a cricket ball, a cyclist at two speeds and a city bus, showing that doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four

slides.narration: The kinetic energy of a body is half its mass times the square of its speed. It is a scalar, it is never negative, and its unit is the joule. Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large. In terms of momentum, kinetic energy is the square of the momentum divided by twice the mass.

slides.heading: The work–energy theorem
slides.body_md: A constant **net** force $F$ acts on a body of mass $m$ along a straight line and changes its speed from $u$ to $v$ over a displacement $S$.
bullets: **Work–energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
Positive net work raises the kinetic energy; negative net work lowers it. The theorem also holds when the force varies (stated here without proof).
slides.narration: Take a constant net force on a body of mass m. Newton's second law gives the force as mass times acceleration, and the equation of motion gives the square of the final speed minus the square of the initial speed as twice the acceleration times the displacement. The work, force times displacement, then equals half m v squared minus half m u squared. The net work done equals the change in kinetic energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: stopping distance of a car
slides.body_md: A car of mass $1200$ kg moving at $20$ m s$^{-1}$ is brought to rest by a constant braking force of $6000$ N. Find the stopping distance, and the distance if the speed were $30$ m s$^{-1}$.
bullets: Work done by the brakes $= -Fs$; final $K = 0$. Theorem: $-Fs = 0 - \tfrac12 mv^{2}$, so $s = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{2F}$.
At $30$ m s$^{-1}$: $s = 90.00$ m. Speed $\times 1.5$ gives distance $\times 2.25$: **$s \propto v^{2}$**.

functions.label: s = ½mv²/F = 0.10 v² (1200 kg, braking force 6000 N)

visual.alt: Stopping distance against initial speed for a 1200 kilogram car braked by a constant force of 6000 newtons: a parabola, 10 metres at 10 metres per second, 40 metres at 20 and 90 metres at 30
visual.caption: Stopping distance grows as the square of the speed.

slides.narration: The brakes do negative work, minus the force times the distance. The car ends at rest, so this equals minus the initial kinetic energy. The distance is the kinetic energy divided by the braking force. At twenty metres per second the kinetic energy is two hundred and forty thousand joules, so the car stops in forty metres. At thirty metres per second it needs ninety metres. The distance grows as the square of the speed.

slides.heading: Potential energy: gravity
slides.body_md: **Potential energy** is the energy a body has because of its position or configuration in a field of a conservative force.
bullets: Lifting a body slowly through a height $h$ needs a force $mg$, so the agent does $mgh$ of work, which is stored as gravitational potential energy (near the Earth, with $g$ constant).
Work done **by gravity** over the same rise is $-mgh$, so $W_{\text{gravity}} = -\Delta U$.
The zero of $U$ is chosen freely; only **differences** of $U$ have meaning.
A $25$ kg can of water raised $6$ m gains $25 \times 9.8 \times 6 = 1470$ J.

slides.narration: Potential energy is energy stored by position. Lifting a body slowly through a height h needs a force equal to its weight, so the work done is m g h, and that is stored as gravitational potential energy. Gravity itself does minus m g h on the way up. The zero level can be chosen freely, because only differences matter. A twenty five kilogram can raised six metres gains one thousand four hundred and seventy joules.

slides.heading: The spring force
slides.body_md: A spring that is stretched or compressed by $x$ from its natural length pulls or pushes back with a **restoring force** (Hooke's law, within the elastic limit):
bullets: $k$ is the **force constant** (stiffness) of the spring in N m$^{-1}$; the minus sign says the force opposes the displacement.
To change the length slowly, the outside agent must apply $+kx$: the force **grows** with the extension, so it is a variable force.
For the spring in the figure $k = 500$ N m$^{-1}$: at $x = 0.12$ m the force is $60$ N, towards the relaxed position.

slides.heading: Conservative and non-conservative forces
slides.body_md: A force is **conservative** if the work it does between two points does not depend on the path, so that the work around any **closed path is zero**.
bullets: **Conservative:** gravity, the force of a spring, the electrostatic force. A potential energy can be defined: $W = -\Delta U$.
**Non-conservative:** friction, air drag, viscous drag. The work depends on the path (and is negative along every part), the work around a closed path is not zero, and no potential energy exists.
Test: is the work the same along every route between the same two points?

slides.narration: A force is conservative if the work it does between two points does not depend on the path taken. Then the work around a closed path is zero, and a potential energy can be defined. Gravity, the spring force and the electrostatic force are conservative. Friction and drag are not. Their work depends on the path, is not zero around a loop, and no potential energy can be assigned.

bullets: Name the angle: $\theta$ is between the **force** and the **displacement**. For a body on a slope, check which angle the question gives.

slides.narration: A stone dropped from a tower speeds up as it falls, yet its potential energy and kinetic energy always add up to the same total. In this part we use that idea for a pendulum, a roller coaster and a spring, meet the energy of mass, and then ask how fast work is done, which is power.

slides.heading: Mechanical energy and its conservation
slides.body_md: The **mechanical energy** of a body is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies: $E = K + U$.
bullets: **Law of conservation of mechanical energy:** if only conservative forces do work, the total mechanical energy stays constant; energy changes form but is not lost.
Friction and drag are non-conservative: they turn mechanical energy into heat, but the **total** energy (including heat) is still conserved.

rows: KE → heat at the brake blocks
Water falling in a hydroelectric dam

visual.alt: Table of energy transformations in five situations and whether mechanical energy is conserved: falling stone, pendulum, spring, braking cyclist and a hydroelectric dam

math: W_{\text{cons}} = \Delta K \quad\text{and}\quad W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta K + \Delta U = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; K + U = \text{constant}
slides.narration: The mechanical energy of a body is its kinetic energy plus its potential energy. The work done by a conservative force equals the gain in kinetic energy and also the loss in potential energy, so the gain in kinetic energy exactly equals the loss in potential energy. If only conservative forces act, the mechanical energy stays constant. Friction turns it into heat, but the total energy is still conserved.

slides.heading: Free fall: energy at every height
slides.body_md: A stone of mass $m$ is released from rest at height $H$. At height $h$ it has fallen $H - h$.
bullets: Potential energy falls and kinetic energy rises by the **same** amount (bars in the figure); the total of $784.0$ J never changes.
On reaching the ground ($h = 0$): $v = \sqrt{2gH} = 28.0$ m s$^{-1}$ for $H = 40$ m.
The speed depends only on the **height fallen**, not on the mass.

slides.heading: The simple pendulum
slides.body_md: A bob of mass $m$ on a string of length $L$ is released from rest at angle $\theta_0$. The tension is always perpendicular to the motion and does **no work**, so only gravity (conservative) does work.
bullets: **At the ends of the swing:** speed zero, kinetic energy zero, potential energy greatest.
**At the lowest point:** potential energy least (taken as zero), kinetic energy greatest, speed greatest.
Energy changes continually between the two; the total stays constant.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: the pendulum bob
slides.body_md: The pendulum of the figure has $L = 1.5$ m, $m = 0.4$ kg and is released from $50^\circ$. Find the speed at the lowest point and at $30^\circ$ from the vertical. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: Height at release: $h = 1.5(1 - \cos 50^\circ) = 0.5358$ m, so $E = mgh = 2.100$ J.
Lowest point: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 0.5358} = 3.24$ m s$^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of the height, potential energy, kinetic energy and speed of the 0.4 kilogram pendulum bob at the release point, at 30 degrees and at the lowest point

slides.narration: At release the bob is zero point five three six metres above the lowest point, so its energy is two point one joules. At the lowest point all of this is kinetic, and the speed is the square root of two g h, which is three point two four metres per second. At thirty degrees from the vertical the bob has dropped less, so its speed is smaller, two point five six metres per second.

slides.heading: The roller coaster
slides.body_md: A car on a frictionless track is released from rest at A. Only gravity does work (the normal reaction is perpendicular to the track), so at any point $v = \sqrt{2g\,(\text{drop below A})}$.
bullets: Speed depends only on the **height**, not on the shape of the track or the mass of the car: B (5 m): 22.1 m s⁻¹; C (18 m): 15.3 m s⁻¹; D (2 m): 23.4 m s⁻¹.
The car can **never rise above the level of A**: at that height its kinetic energy would be zero.
In practice friction and air drag are non-conservative, so real cars lose mechanical energy as heat and the first hill must be the highest.

slides.heading: The oscillating spring: U + K = E
slides.body_md: A block of mass $m$ on a smooth horizontal surface is joined to a spring of force constant $k$ and released from rest at $x = A$. Only the spring force (conservative) does work.
bullets: The block starts from rest, so by the work–energy theorem the work of the spring equals the kinetic energy gained. $U + K$ has the same value at every $x$.
$E = \tfrac12 kA^2$ is fixed by the amplitude. Maximum speed (at $x = 0$): $v_{\max} = A\sqrt{k/m}$.
Preview of the Oscillations chapter: with $x = A\cos\omega t$ and $\omega^2 = k/m$, $U = \tfrac12 kA^2\cos^2\omega t$ and $K = \tfrac12 kA^2\sin^2\omega t$ add to the same $\tfrac12 kA^2$.

math: \tfrac12 mv^{2} - 0 = \tfrac12 k\,(A^{2} - x^{2}) \;\Rightarrow\; \tfrac12 kx^{2} + \tfrac12 mv^{2} = \tfrac12 kA^{2}
slides.narration: A block on a smooth surface is joined to a spring and released from rest at the amplitude A. As it moves in to a displacement x, the spring does work equal to half k times A squared minus x squared. The block started from rest, so this work is its kinetic energy. Adding the stored energy, half k x squared, the total is always half k A squared. The potential and kinetic energies always add up to the same total.

slides.heading: Energy graphs against displacement
slides.body_md: Using $U = \tfrac12 kx^2$ and $K = E - \tfrac12 kx^2$ with $E = \tfrac12 kA^2$:
bullets: **U against x:** an upward parabola, zero at $x = 0$, equal to $E$ at $x = \pm A$.
**K against x:** the inverted parabola, equal to $E$ at $x = 0$ and zero at the turning points $x = \pm A$.
**E:** a horizontal line. $U$ and $K$ cross where each is $E/2$, at $x = \pm A/\sqrt{2}$ (here $\pm0.0566$ m).
The body can never be found where $U > E$, since that would need negative kinetic energy.

visual.alt: Energies against displacement for a 0.4 kilogram block on a 250 newton per metre spring with amplitude 0.08 metres: the potential energy is an upward parabola from zero at the centre to 0.8 joules at each end, the kinetic energy is the downward parabola from 0.8 joules at the centre to zero at the ends, and the total is the horizontal line at 0.8 joules
visual.caption: U is a parabola, K an inverted parabola, E a horizontal line.

slides.narration: Plot the energies against the displacement. The potential energy is an upward parabola, zero at the centre and equal to the total at the ends. The kinetic energy is the inverted parabola, equal to the total at the centre and zero at the ends. The total energy is a horizontal line. The two curves cross where each is half the total, at the amplitude divided by the square root of two.

slides.heading: Preview: energy graphs against time
slides.body_md: Since $x = A\cos\omega t$: $U = E\cos^{2}\omega t$ and $K = E\sin^{2}\omega t$. Each oscillates between $0$ and $E$, **out of step**.
bullets: Both repeat twice in every period $T$ of the motion: they change at **twice the frequency** of the block. Here $T = 2\pi/\omega = 0.251$ s.
When $U$ is largest $K$ is zero and the reverse; energy flows back and forth between the spring and the block.
Their sum, $E = 0.80$ J, is a steady horizontal line.
This uses $x = A\cos\omega t$ from the Oscillations chapter; in this chapter the graphs against $x$ are the ones to know.

visual.caption: U and K swap twice every period; their sum is steady.

slides.narration: Plotted against time, the potential energy is E cosine squared omega t and the kinetic energy is E sine squared omega t. They rise and fall out of step, each between zero and the total. Both go through two full cycles in one period of the block, so they vary at twice its frequency. When one is at its largest the other is zero, and their sum is the steady total of zero point eight joules. This is a preview of the oscillations chapter.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: the oscillating block
slides.body_md: A $0.4$ kg block on a smooth surface is joined to a spring of $k = 250$ N m$^{-1}$ and oscillates with amplitude $0.08$ m. Find (i) the total energy, (ii) the maximum speed, (iii) $U$, $K$ and the speed at $x = 0.05$ m.
bullets: (i) $E = \tfrac12 kA^2 = \tfrac12 \times 250 \times 0.08^2 = 0.800$ J.
(ii) At $x = 0$ all is kinetic: $\tfrac12 mv_{\max}^2 = E$, so $v_{\max} = \sqrt{2 \times 0.800 / 0.4} = 2.00$ m s$^{-1}$.

slides.heading: Mass–energy equivalence: E = mc²
slides.body_md: Einstein showed that mass is a form of energy. A mass $m$ (that disappears) is equivalent to an energy:
bullets: This is a **statement** here; it is not derived in this course.
Because $c^2 = 9.0 \times 10^{16}$ m$^2$ s$^{-2}$ is so large, a tiny mass is equivalent to a huge energy.
In nuclear reactions the total mass of the products is slightly less than that of the reactants; the **mass defect** appears as energy, which powers reactors and the Sun.
In everyday chemical and mechanical processes the change of mass is far too small to notice.

slides.heading: Power
slides.body_md: **Power** is the rate of doing work (or of transferring energy). The **average power** over a time $t$ is:
bullets: SI unit: the **watt** (W), $1$ W $= 1$ J s$^{-1}$. Dimensions $[\text{M}\,\text{L}^{2}\,\text{T}^{-3}]$. Power is a scalar.
Instantaneous power is $P = \dfrac{dW}{dt}$, the power at a particular instant.
A **kilowatt hour** is a unit of **energy**: $1$ kW h $= 3.6 \times 10^{6}$ J. A $100$ W bulb used for $10$ h consumes $1.0$ kW h, one unit on the electricity bill.

slides.narration: Power is the rate of doing work, the work done divided by the time taken. Its unit is the watt, one joule per second. Instantaneous power is the rate at one instant. A kilowatt hour is a unit of energy, not of power, and it equals three point six million joules. A one hundred watt bulb used for ten hours consumes one unit on the electricity bill.

slides.heading: Power and velocity: P = F·v
slides.body_md: A constant force $F$ acting along the displacement $dS$ in a time $dt$ does work $dW = F\,dS$. Dividing by $dt$:
bullets: For a force along the velocity, $P = Fv$: for a given power, a **greater speed needs a smaller force**, which is why a vehicle climbs a hill in low gear.
At a **constant speed** the driving force equals the resistive force, so $P = F_{\text{resist}} \times v$.
Plot: for a steady force the power is a straight line through the origin in $v$.

slides.narration: A force F acts through a small distance in a small time. Work is force times distance, so dividing by the time, the power equals the force times the velocity. For a given power, a higher speed needs a smaller force, which is why a vehicle climbs a hill in low gear. At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, so the power equals that force times the speed.

slides.body_md: (i) A lift with its load has a mass of $1000$ kg and rises at a steady $1.5$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the power of the motor, ignoring friction. (ii) A pump raises $1500$ kg of water through $20$ m in $600$ s. Find its average power. ($g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.)
bullets: (i) At constant speed the cable force equals the weight: $F = Mg = 1000 \times 9.8 = 9800$ N. $P = Fv = 9800 \times 1.5 = 14700$ W $= 14.7$ kW.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Choose the **zero of potential energy** first and say so; write the energy at the start and the end, then equate. Remember the string tension and the normal reaction do no work.
For the oscillator, show $U + K = E$ from the work done by the spring, $\tfrac12 k(A^2 - x^2) = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Graphs: label axes, mark $E$, $\pm A$, and the crossing at $E/2$.
Use $E = mc^2$ with $m$ in **kilograms** and $c = 3 \times 10^8$ m s$^{-1}$; the answer is in joules. Do not derive it.
Power: say whether it is **average** ($W/t$) or **instantaneous** ($Fv$). At constant speed driving force = resistive force. Convert kW h to joules with $3.6 \times 10^6$.

Common mistakes: using the length of the string instead of the height for the pendulum; forgetting that mechanical energy is lost to heat when friction acts; confusing kilowatt (power) with kilowatt hour (energy).

sections.heading: 1. Work done by a constant force and by a variable force
sections.body_md:
- **Work** is done when a force moves its point of application; only the component of the force **along the displacement** counts. It is a **scalar**; the SI unit is the **joule** ($1$ J $= 1$ N m); in CGS the **erg**, with $1$ J $= 10^7$ erg. Dimensions $[\text{M}\,\text{L}^2\,\text{T}^{-2}]$.
- **Constant force:** $W = \vec F\cdot\vec S = FS\cos\theta$, with $\theta$ the angle between the force and the **displacement** (not the path length). A 90 N pull at 35° through 12 m does 884.7 J; the perpendicular component 51.6 N does none.
- **Sign:** positive for $\theta < 90^\circ$, zero for $\theta = 90^\circ$ (a trunk carried along a level platform, the centripetal force on a body moving in a circle), negative for $\theta > 90^\circ$ (friction, brakes, gravity on a rising ball).
- **Variable force:** divide the path into strips $\Delta S$, $\Delta W = F\Delta S$, so $W = \int F\,dS$ = the **area under the F–S graph**; area below the axis is negative. The handcart graph splits into a triangle (30 J), a rectangle (120 J) and a trapezium (60 J): 210 J.

key_terms.definition_md: The scalar product of the force and the displacement, W = F·S = FS cos θ; unit joule.
The work done by a force of 1 N when the body moves 1 m along the force; 1 J = 10⁷ erg.
F·S = FS cos θ: a number, with no direction.
A force whose size changes along the path; its work is the area under the F–S graph.

sections.heading: 2. Kinetic energy and the work–energy theorem
sections.body_md:
- **Kinetic energy** $K = \tfrac12 mv^2$: a scalar, never negative, proportional to the **square** of the speed (double the speed, four times the energy). In terms of momentum, $K = p^2/2m$.
- **Work–energy theorem (constant force):** with $F = ma$ and $v^2 - u^2 = 2aS$: $W = FS = maS = \tfrac12 m(v^2 - u^2) = K_f - K_i$. **Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.** (It also holds for a variable force.)
- **Stopping distance:** brakes do $-Fs$ and the final $K$ is zero, so $s = \dfrac{mv^2}{2F}$, proportional to $v^2$. A 1200 kg car braked by 6000 N stops from 20 m s⁻¹ in 40.0 m and from 30 m s⁻¹ in 90.0 m (2.25 times as far for 1.5 times the speed).

The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.

sections.heading: 3. Potential energy, the spring and conservative forces
sections.body_md:
- **Potential energy** $U$ is energy stored by position or configuration in a field of a **conservative** force; $W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U$. Near the Earth, $U = mgh$ relative to a chosen zero; only **differences** matter (a 2 kg ball: 29.40 J on the shelf and 15.68 J on the table above the floor, but always 13.72 J apart). A 25 kg can raised 6 m gains 1470 J.
- **Spring:** $F = -kx$ (Hooke's law); the applied force grows from $0$ to $kx$, so the work is the area of the triangle, $W = \tfrac12 x \cdot kx = \tfrac12 kx^2$; by integration $\int_0^x kx'\,dx' = \tfrac12 kx^2$. This is stored as $U = \tfrac12 kx^2$ (stretch or compression). For $k = 500$ N m⁻¹: 0.400 J at 0.04 m, 1.60 J at 0.08 m, 3.60 J at 0.12 m; the stretch from 0.04 m to 0.12 m needs 3.20 J.
- **Conservative force:** the work between two points is **independent of the path**; the work round a closed path is **zero**; a potential energy exists. Examples: gravity, the spring force, the electrostatic force.
- **Non-conservative force:** the work depends on the path; round a closed path it is not zero; no potential energy; examples: friction, air drag, viscous drag. Gravity does −588 J on a 12 kg load raised 5 m by either route; a 40 N friction does −520 J or −680 J on two routes.

key_terms.definition_md: Energy stored by position or configuration, defined for conservative forces; W = −ΔU.

sections.heading: 4. Conservation of mechanical energy, the oscillating spring and E = mc²
sections.body_md:
- **Conservation:** if only conservative forces do work, $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$ and $E = K + U$ is constant. Friction turns mechanical energy into heat, but the **total** energy is conserved.
- **Free fall:** $mgH = mgh + \tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2g(H-h)}$, independent of mass. The 2 kg stone from 40 m has $E = 784.0$ J; at 15 m it moves at 22.1 m s⁻¹ and it lands at 28.0 m s⁻¹.
- **Pendulum:** tension does no work; $v = \sqrt{2gL(1-\cos\theta_0)}$ at the lowest point: 3.24 m s⁻¹ for $L = 1.5$ m, 50°.
- **Roller coaster:** $v = \sqrt{2g\,(\text{drop})}$; the car cannot rise above its starting level (speeds 22.1, 15.3, 23.4 m s⁻¹ at B, C, D).
- **Oscillating spring:** released from rest at $x = A$, the block moves to $x$ while the spring does work $\int_A^x (-kx')\,dx' = \tfrac12 k(A^2 - x^2)$; by the work–energy theorem this is the kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2$, so $U + K = \tfrac12 kx^2 + \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 kA^2$, the same at every $x$. For 0.4 kg, $k = 250$ N m⁻¹, $A = 0.08$ m: $E = 0.800$ J, $v_{\max} = 2.00$ m s⁻¹.
- **Energy graphs:** against $x$, $U$ is an upward parabola, $K$ an inverted parabola, $E$ a horizontal line, crossing at $E/2$ where $x = \pm A/\sqrt2$. Against time (a preview of the Oscillations chapter, which gives $x = A\cos\omega t$), $U = E\cos^2\omega t$ and $K = E\sin^2\omega t$, out of step, at twice the frequency of the block.
- **Mass–energy (statement only):** $E = mc^2$ with $c = 3.0 \times 10^8$ m s⁻¹, so a mass of 2.5 mg is equivalent to 2.25 × 10¹¹ J (about 71 years of a 100 W bulb). The derivation is not required.

sections.heading: 5. Power
sections.body_md:
- **Power** is the rate of doing work: average $P = W/t$; instantaneous $P = dW/dt$. Unit the **watt** ($1$ W $= 1$ J s⁻¹); $1$ kW $= 10^3$ W, $1$ hp $= 746$ W. Dimensions $[\text{M}\,\text{L}^2\,\text{T}^{-3}]$.
- **P = F·v:** $dW = F\,dS$, so $P = F\,dS/dt = \vec F\cdot\vec v = Fv\cos\theta$. For a given power a higher speed needs a smaller force. At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force.
- **Examples:** a lift of 1000 kg rising at 1.5 m s⁻¹ needs 14700 W; a pump raising 1500 kg of water 20 m in 600 s delivers 490 W; a car at 25 m s⁻¹ against 1400 N needs 35.0 kW.
- **Kilowatt hour:** a unit of **energy**, $1$ kW h $= 3.6\times10^6$ J; a 100 W bulb for 10 h uses 1.0 kW h.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Work is F S cos θ with θ between the force and the displacement; say whether the work is positive, zero or negative. Friction and brakes do negative work.
- Work–energy theorem: net work = change in kinetic energy. Stopping distance s = mv²/2F, proportional to v².
- U = ½kx²: show the triangle area or the integral of kx; the spring force is F = −kx.
- Conservative: work independent of the path, zero on a closed path (gravity, spring). Non-conservative: friction, drag.
- Mechanical energy is conserved only when no friction or drag acts; tension and the normal reaction do no work. Choose the zero of U and state it.
- Oscillating spring: ½kx² + ½mv² = ½kA². E = mc² is a statement; use kilograms and joules.
- P = W/t is average power, P = F·v instantaneous. 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, a unit of energy.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

cards.front_md: Define work done by a constant force.
cards.back_md: The scalar product of the force and the displacement: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec S = FS\cos\theta$; unit joule.

cards.front_md: Define the joule and relate it to the erg.
cards.back_md: The work done when a force of 1 N moves a body 1 m along the force; $1\ \text{J} = 10^{7}$ erg.

cards.front_md: When is the work done by a force zero even though the force is not zero?
cards.back_md: When the force is perpendicular to the displacement ($\theta = 90^\circ$), or when there is no displacement.

cards.front_md: When is work negative? Give an example.
cards.back_md: When $90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$: the force opposes the motion, as friction does on a sliding block.

cards.front_md: How is the work done by a variable force found from a graph?
cards.back_md: It is the area under the force–displacement graph, $W = \int F\,dS$; area below the axis is negative.

cards.front_md: Work of a 90 N force at 35° to a 12 m displacement?
cards.back_md: $W = 90 \times 12 \times \cos 35^\circ = 884.7$ J.

cards.front_md: Write the kinetic energy of a body in terms of mass and speed, and of momentum.
cards.back_md: $K = \tfrac12 mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$.

cards.front_md: State the work–energy theorem.
cards.back_md: The net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = K_f - K_i$.

cards.front_md: Outline the derivation of the work–energy theorem for a constant force.
cards.back_md: From $F = ma$ and $v^2 - u^2 = 2aS$: $W = FS = maS = \tfrac12 m(v^2 - u^2)$.

cards.front_md: Write the stopping distance of a vehicle braked by a constant force $F$.
cards.back_md: $s = \dfrac{mv^2}{2F}$, proportional to the square of the speed.

cards.front_md: If the speed of a car is doubled, how does its stopping distance change (same brakes)?
cards.back_md: It becomes four times as large.

cards.front_md: Stopping distance of 1200 kg at 20 m/s with a 6000 N braking force?
cards.back_md: $s = \dfrac{\tfrac12 \times 1200 \times 20^2}{6000} = 40.0$ m.

cards.front_md: Define potential energy.
cards.back_md: Energy stored in a body because of its position or configuration in a field of a conservative force; $W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U$.

cards.front_md: Write the gravitational potential energy near the Earth.
cards.back_md: $U = mgh$, measured from a chosen zero level; only differences of $U$ matter.

cards.front_md: State Hooke's law for a spring.
cards.back_md: $F = -kx$: the restoring force is proportional to the extension and opposes it; $k$ is in N m$^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: Derive the energy stored in a stretched spring by area.
cards.back_md: The force grows from 0 to $kx$, so the work is the area of the triangle, $\tfrac12 \cdot x \cdot kx = \tfrac12 kx^2$.

cards.front_md: Derive the energy stored in a stretched spring by integration.
cards.back_md: $W = \int_0^x kx'\,dx' = \left[\tfrac12 kx'^2\right]_0^x = \tfrac12 kx^2$.

cards.front_md: Is the energy stored in a compressed spring different from that of an equal stretch?
cards.back_md: No: $U = \tfrac12 kx^2$ depends on $x^2$, so it is the same.

cards.front_md: Define a conservative force and give two examples.
cards.back_md: A force whose work between two points does not depend on the path (zero round a closed path): gravity and the spring force.

cards.front_md: Why is friction non-conservative?
cards.back_md: Its work depends on the path (negative along every part), is not zero round a closed path, and no potential energy exists.

cards.front_md: State the law of conservation of mechanical energy.
cards.back_md: If only conservative forces do work, the sum of kinetic and potential energy of the body stays constant.

cards.front_md: Write the speed of a body after falling through a height $h$ from rest (no air).
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, independent of the mass.

cards.front_md: Why does the tension in a pendulum do no work?
cards.back_md: It is always perpendicular to the motion of the bob.

cards.front_md: Write the speed of a pendulum bob at the lowest point, released at angle $\theta_0$.
cards.back_md: $v = \sqrt{2gL(1-\cos\theta_0)}$.

cards.front_md: Show that $U + K$ is constant for a mass on a spring.
cards.back_md: Released from rest at $x = A$, the spring does work $\tfrac12 k(A^2 - x^2)$ as the block moves to $x$; this equals $\tfrac12 mv^2$, so $\tfrac12 kx^2 + \tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 kA^2$.

cards.front_md: Describe the graphs of $U$, $K$ and $E$ against $x$ for an oscillating spring.
cards.back_md: $U$: upward parabola; $K$: inverted parabola; $E$: horizontal line; $U = K = E/2$ at $x = \pm A/\sqrt2$.

cards.front_md: State the mass–energy relation and the meaning of its symbols.
cards.back_md: $E = mc^2$: a mass $m$ is equivalent to energy $E$; $c = 3.0 \times 10^8$ m s$^{-1}$ is the speed of light.

cards.front_md: Define power and its SI unit.
cards.back_md: The rate of doing work, $P = W/t$; the watt, $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J s}^{-1}$.

cards.front_md: Derive $P = Fv$.
cards.back_md: $P = dW/dt = F\,dS/dt = Fv$ for a force along the velocity; in general $\vec F\cdot\vec v$.

cards.front_md: How many joules in one kilowatt hour?
cards.back_md: $1\ \text{kW h} = 10^3\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J; it is a unit of energy.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A railway porter carries a trunk on his head along a level platform at constant speed. The work done on the trunk by the force that his head exerts on it is

options.text_md: positive, because he spends effort to carry it
positive, equal to the weight of the trunk times the distance walked
zero, because the force is perpendicular to the displacement
negative, because the trunk is carried against gravity

questions.solution_md: The head pushes the trunk upward, to balance its weight, while the displacement is horizontal. The angle between them is 90 degrees, so W = FS cos 90° = 0. Effort or tiredness does not count as work in physics.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A bullock pulls a cart along a straight level road through 25 m with a rope that exerts a constant tension of 400 N at 30° above the road. The work done by the rope is
questions.solution_md: Only the component of the tension along the road does work: W = 400 × 25 × cos 30° = 8660 J. Using the full tension gives the larger value 10000 J, and the sine gives the component across the road.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A fielder stops a fast cricket ball by drawing his hands back with the ball as it slows. During this stopping the work done on the ball by the fielder’s hands is

options.text_md: positive, because the ball is brought to rest
zero, because the ball finally has no velocity
positive, because the hands do work in stopping it
negative, because the force on the ball is opposite to its displacement

questions.solution_md: The hands push against the ball’s motion, so the force and the displacement are in opposite directions (θ = 180°) and the work is negative: the ball loses kinetic energy.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The force on a sled rises uniformly from zero to 18 N over the first 4 m of its path and then stays at 18 N for the next 3 m. The work done over the whole 7 m is
questions.solution_md: Work is the area under the F–S graph: a triangle of ½ × 4 × 18 = 36 J, then a rectangle of 18 × 3 = 54 J. The total is 90 J; treating the whole path as a rectangle overestimates it.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of work, the joule, is related to the CGS unit, the erg, by
questions.solution_md: 1 J = 1 N m = 10⁵ dyne × 10² cm = 10⁷ dyne cm = 10⁷ erg.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A force of 20 N acts on a body that is displaced 3 m in a direction making 120° with the force. The work done by the force is
questions.solution_md: cos 120° = −0.5, so W = 20 × 3 × (−0.5) = −30.0 J. The sign is negative because the angle is obtuse: the force has a component against the displacement.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The speed of a body is tripled. Its kinetic energy becomes
questions.solution_md: K = ½mv² depends on the square of the speed, so tripling v multiplies K by 3² = 9.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A loaded truck of mass 4000 kg and a car of mass 1000 kg move with the same momentum. The ratio (kinetic energy of the car) : (kinetic energy of the truck) is
questions.solution_md: K = p²/(2m). With the same p, K is inversely proportional to the mass, so the car has 4 times the kinetic energy of the truck.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: According to the work–energy theorem, the net work done on a body is equal to

options.text_md: the force multiplied by the time for which it acts
the change in its kinetic energy

questions.solution_md: The theorem states W(net) = K(final) − K(initial). The final kinetic energy alone is equal to the work only when the body starts from rest.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: With its brakes applying a constant retarding force, a car moving at 10 m s⁻¹ stops in 12 m. Using the same brakes, the distance in which it stops from 30 m s⁻¹ is
questions.solution_md: Fs = ½mv² with the same F and m gives s proportional to v². The speed is multiplied by 3, so the distance is multiplied by 9: 12 × 9 = 108 m.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A stone of mass 0.5 kg has a kinetic energy of 36 J. Its speed is
questions.solution_md: K = ½mv², so v = √(2K/m) = √(2 × 36 / 0.5) = √144 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. The value 144 is v² and still needs its square root.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A spring is first stretched by 2 cm and then, separately, compressed by 2 cm from its natural length. The energy stored in the compressed spring, compared with that in the stretched spring, is

options.text_md: equal, because U = ½kx² depends on x²
smaller, because the coils are pushed together
larger, because compression is harder than stretching

questions.solution_md: U = ½kx². The extension x enters through its square, so a compression of 2 cm stores exactly the same energy as a stretch of 2 cm.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A spring of force constant 200 N m⁻¹ is stretched by 5 cm. It is then stretched a further 5 cm. The work done in the second stretch is how many times the work done in the first?
questions.solution_md: The first stretch stores ½k(0.05)² = 0.250 J. At 0.10 m the energy is four times as large, so the second stretch adds 4 − 1 = 3 times the first: 0.750 J, a ratio of 3.

marking_scheme.step: W₁ = ½kx² and W₂ = ½k(2x)² − ½kx² = 3 × ½kx², so W₂/W₁ = 3 (c)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a conservative force is correct?

options.text_md: The work it does depends on the path between the two points
It always acts opposite to the velocity of the body
The work it does round any closed path is zero
It can only act on a body that is at rest

questions.solution_md: For a conservative force the work between two points is the same for every path, so the work round a closed path is zero. A force that always opposes the velocity, such as friction, is non-conservative.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Which of the following forces is non-conservative?

options.text_md: The weight of a body near the Earth
The air drag on a parachutist coming down
The force of a stretched spring
The electrostatic force between two point charges

questions.solution_md: Drag depends on how the body moves, opposes the motion along the whole path and turns mechanical energy into heat, so the work depends on the path. Gravity, the spring force and the electrostatic force are conservative.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A book of mass 3 kg lies on a shelf 2.0 m above the floor. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², its potential energy relative to a table top 0.75 m above the floor is
questions.solution_md: Relative to the table the book is 1.25 m higher, so U = mgh = 3 × 9.8 × 1.25 = 36.75 J. The value 58.80 J is the energy relative to the floor.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A ball is dropped from rest from a height H above the ground. Ignoring air resistance, the height above the ground at which its kinetic energy equals its potential energy is
questions.solution_md: The total energy mgH stays constant. K = U means each equals half of it, so mgh = ½mgH and h = H/2, taking the ground as the zero of potential energy.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A simple pendulum bob is released from rest at one end of its swing. Neglecting air resistance, the kinetic energy of the bob is greatest

options.text_md: when the bob is at the end of its swing
when the string makes 45° with the vertical on its way down
when the bob passes through the lowest point
at every point, since the string tension keeps it moving

questions.solution_md: Mechanical energy is constant, so the kinetic energy is greatest where the potential energy is least: at the lowest point. At the ends the bob is momentarily at rest and K = 0.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: Two cars of masses 500 kg and 900 kg are released from rest from the same height on a frictionless roller-coaster track. At the bottom of the track their speeds are

options.text_md: equal, because the speed depends only on the height descended
greater for the 900 kg car, because it has more potential energy
greater for the 500 kg car, because it is lighter
zero for both, because they start from rest

questions.solution_md: mgh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gh): the mass cancels. The heavier car has more energy to convert, but also more mass to speed up, so both reach the same speed.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A block oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface at the end of a spring with amplitude A. When its displacement from the equilibrium position is A/2, the fraction of the total energy that is kinetic is
questions.solution_md: At x = A/2 the potential energy is ½k(A/2)² = ¼ × ½kA² = E/4, so the kinetic energy is E − E/4 = 3E/4.

marking_scheme.step: U = ½k(A/2)² = ¼ of ½kA², so K = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 of E (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A mass of 0.20 g is completely converted into energy. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the energy released is
questions.solution_md: The mass must be in kilograms: 0.20 g = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg. E = mc² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 9.0 × 10¹⁶ = 1.8 × 10¹³ J. Using 0.20 as kilograms would give a thousand times too much.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: The SI unit of power, the watt, expressed in base units is
questions.solution_md: P = W/t, so 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹ and 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻². Hence 1 W = 1 kg m² s⁻³.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A motor lifts a 250 kg load through 12 m at a constant speed in 20 s. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², the useful power of the motor is
questions.solution_md: The work done is mgh = 250 × 9.8 × 12 = 29400 J. Dividing by the time, P = 29400 / 20 = 1470 W. Equivalently, F v = 2450 × 0.6.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A locomotive working at constant power hauls a train at 20 m s⁻¹ on level track. On a slope the pulling force it must exert is doubled. The speed of the train is now
questions.solution_md: P = Fv. At constant power, doubling F halves v: 20 / 2 = 10 m s⁻¹. A large pulling force is possible only at low speed.

marking_scheme.step: P = Fv is constant, so v = 20 / 2 = 10 m s⁻¹ (a)

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md: A 2 kW electric heater runs for 3 h. The energy it consumes, in joules, is
questions.solution_md: E = Pt = 2000 W × 3 × 3600 s = 2.16 × 10⁷ J, which is 6 kW h (1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J). The value 6.00 × 10³ J forgets to convert the hours to seconds.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A porter carrying a suitcase on his head along a level platform does no work on the suitcase in the physical sense.

**Reason (R):** The force that supports the suitcase is vertical and the displacement is horizontal, so the force is perpendicular to the displacement.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is true and explains it: with θ = 90° the work W = FS cos θ is zero.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a compressed spring pushes a block back to the natural length, the spring does positive work on the block.

**Reason (R):** Work is a scalar quantity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the spring force and the displacement of the block are in the same direction. R is also true, but being a scalar does not say why the work is positive; the sign follows from the angle between the force and the displacement. So R is not the explanation.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a constant kinetic energy.

**Reason (R):** The force directed towards the centre does positive work on the body.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the speed is constant, so K = ½mv² is constant. R is false: the force towards the centre is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. This is also why the kinetic energy does not change.

provenance.author: claude-sonnet-5-5 (subject-producer chapter writer; reviewed by claude-opus-5-5)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The work done by kinetic friction on a block that slides round a closed loop and returns to its starting point is zero.

**Reason (R):** Friction is a non-conservative force.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.

questions.stem_md: A roller-coaster car of mass 600 kg is released from rest at A, 28 m above the lowest point of the track. Neglecting friction and air drag, and taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the speed of the car at B, 8 m above the lowest point, and its kinetic energy there.

answer.model_answer_md: Only gravity does work, since the normal reaction is perpendicular to the track, so mechanical energy is conserved. From A to B the car drops $28 - 8 = 20$ m. Then $\tfrac12 mv^2 = mg\,(\text{drop})$, so $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 20} = 19.8$ m s$^{-1}$, independent of the mass. The kinetic energy is $K = mg \times 20 = 600 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 117600$ J.

questions.solution_md: Speed from the drop below A; mass cancels.

marking_scheme.step: Drop from A to B = 20 m; energy conserved

questions.stem_md: A spring of force constant 1200 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 3 cm from its natural length and then compressed by a further 3 cm. Find the energy stored in the spring at each of the two stages and the work done during the second compression.

answer.model_answer_md: The energy stored in a spring is $U = \tfrac12 kx^2$ for a stretch or a compression. At $0.03$ m it is $\tfrac12 \times 1200 \times 0.03^2 = 0.540$ J. At $0.06$ m it is $\tfrac12 \times 1200 \times 0.06^2 = 2.16$ J. The work done in the second compression is the increase in the stored energy, $2.16 - 0.540 = 1.62$ J, three times the first.

questions.solution_md: U = ½kx² at each stage; the work is the difference.

marking_scheme.step: Work in the second compression = 1.62 J

questions.stem_md: A mass of 1.0 mg is converted completely into energy in a nuclear process. Taking the speed of light as 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, find (i) the energy released and (ii) the time for which this energy could supply a power station of output 100 MW.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The mass must first be written in kilograms: $1.0\ \text{mg} = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ kg. Then $E = mc^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6} \times (3.0 \times 10^8)^2 = 9.0 \times 10^{10}$ J. (ii) Power is energy delivered per unit time, so the time for which this energy can supply the power station is $t = E/P = 9.0 \times 10^{10} / (100 \times 10^{6}) = 900$ s, which is $15$ minutes: a tiny mass runs a large station for a quarter of an hour.

questions.solution_md: E = mc² in kg, then t = E/P.

questions.stem_md: A crane lifts a load of 800 kg vertically at a steady 0.5 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find (i) the power the crane delivers to the load and (ii) the work it does on the load in 40 s.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) At a steady speed there is no acceleration, so the upward force of the cable equals the weight of the load, $F = mg = 800 \times 9.8 = 7840$ N. The power delivered is $P = Fv = 7840 \times 0.5 = 3920$ W. (ii) The work done in 40 s is $W = Pt = 3920 \times 40 = 156800$ J, which is the same as $mgh$ for the height of $20$ m gained in that time.

questions.solution_md: F equals the weight at steady speed; W = Pt.

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the work–energy theorem for a body acted on by a constant net force along a straight line. [3] (b) A bus of mass 8000 kg moving at 15 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest in 50 m by a constant braking force. Find the force, and the distance in which the same force would stop the bus from 10 m s⁻¹. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let a constant net force $F$ change the speed of a body of mass $m$ from $u$ to $v$ over a displacement $S$. Then $F = ma$, and the equation of motion gives $v^2 - u^2 = 2aS$. The work done is $W = FS = maS = \tfrac12 mv^2 - \tfrac12 mu^2$, so the net work done equals the change in kinetic energy.

(b) The brakes remove the kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2 = \tfrac12 \times 8000 \times 15^2 = 900000$ J over 50 m, so $F = 900000 / 50 = 18000$ N. At 10 m s$^{-1}$ the kinetic energy is $400000$ J, so $s = 400000 / 18000 = 22.2$ m.

questions.solution_md: Derivation from F = ma and v² − u² = 2aS, then Fs = ½mv².

marking_scheme.step: Net work = change in kinetic energy

questions.stem_md: (a) Show, using the area under the force–extension graph, that the work done in stretching a spring of force constant k through an extension x is ½kx², and confirm the result by integration. [3] (b) A spring has k = 400 N m⁻¹. Find the force needed to hold it stretched by 5 cm, and the extra work done in stretching it from 5 cm to 8 cm. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The applied force grows steadily from $0$ to $kx$, so the graph of force against extension is a straight line through the origin. The work done equals the area under it, a triangle of base $x$ and height $kx$, which is $\tfrac12 \times x \times kx = \tfrac12 kx^2$. By integration, $W = \int_0^x kx'\,dx' = \tfrac12 kx^2$, and this is stored as potential energy.

(b) The force at 5 cm is $F = kx = 400 \times 0.05 = 20.0$ N. The stored energies are $U_1 = \tfrac12 \times 400 \times 0.05^2 = 0.500$ J and $U_2 = \tfrac12 \times 400 \times 0.08^2 = 1.28$ J, so the extra work is $1.28 - 0.500 = 0.780$ J.

questions.solution_md: Area of the triangle and the integral of kx; then the difference of U.

marking_scheme.step: Force rises from 0 to kx linearly; work = area of the triangle
Integral of kx′ from 0 to x = ½kx²; stored as potential energy

questions.stem_md: (a) Distinguish between a conservative and a non-conservative force, giving one example of each. [2] (b) A 15 kg block is raised through 4.0 m, first vertically and then along a smooth ramp 10 m long. Find the work done by gravity on each route (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). [1] (c) A box is dragged from P to Q against a constant friction force of 30 N, first straight (10 m) and then along two perpendicular sides of lengths 6 m and 8 m. Find the work done by friction on each route and say what the results show. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The work done by a conservative force between two points is independent of the path, so it is zero round a closed path, and a potential energy can be defined; gravity and the spring force are examples. The work of a non-conservative force depends on the path and no potential energy exists; friction and air drag are examples.

(b) Gravity does $-mgh = -15 \times 9.8 \times 4.0 = -588.0$ J on the vertical route, and the same $-588.0$ J up the ramp.

(c) Friction does $-30 \times 10 = -300$ J on the straight route and $-30 \times 14 = -420$ J on the other route. The work depends on the path, which shows that friction is non-conservative.

questions.solution_md: Path independence for gravity; friction work equals force times path length.

marking_scheme.step: Conservative: work independent of the path, zero on a closed path; example gravity or spring
Non-conservative: work depends on the path; example friction or drag
Friction: −300 J straight and −420 J round the corner

questions.stem_md: (a) A simple pendulum bob is released from rest at one end of its swing. Describe the energy changes during half a swing, and explain why the tension in the string does no work. [2] (b) A bob of mass 0.5 kg on a string 1.5 m long is released from rest with the string at 40° to the vertical. Find its total mechanical energy relative to the lowest point, its speed at the lowest point, and its speed when the string is at 20° to the vertical on the way down (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At the release point the bob is at rest and its energy is all potential. As it swings down the potential energy decreases and the kinetic energy increases by the same amount, reaching the greatest kinetic energy at the lowest point. The tension is always perpendicular to the velocity of the bob, so it does no work and only gravity changes the energy.

(b) At release $h_0 = 1.5(1 - \cos 40^\circ) = 0.3509$ m, so $E = mgh_0 = 0.5 \times 9.8 \times 0.3509 = 1.720$ J. At the lowest point $v = \sqrt{2gh_0} = 2.623$ m s$^{-1}$. At 20° the height is $h_1 = 0.09046$ m, so $v = \sqrt{2g(h_0 - h_1)} = 2.259$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Energy conserved; speed from the drop in height.

marking_scheme.step: Potential energy changes into kinetic energy; K greatest at the lowest point, total constant
Tension perpendicular to the velocity, so zero work

questions.stem_md: A block of mass m on a smooth horizontal surface is attached to a spring of force constant k and oscillates with amplitude A. (a) Show that its total energy is ½kA² at every displacement x. [2] (b) Describe the graphs of the potential, kinetic and total energies against x. [1] (c) For m = 0.25 kg, k = 100 N m⁻¹ and A = 0.1 m, find the total energy and the maximum speed, and the speed at x = 0.06 m. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The block is released from rest at $x = A$, where the energy is all potential, $\tfrac12 kA^2$. The work done by the spring from $A$ to $x$ is $\tfrac12 k(A^2 - x^2)$, which by the work–energy theorem equals the kinetic energy $\tfrac12 mv^2$. Hence $\tfrac12 mv^2 + \tfrac12 kx^2 = \tfrac12 kA^2$ at every $x$.

(b) $U = \tfrac12 kx^2$ is an upward parabola, $K = \tfrac12 k(A^2 - x^2)$ is an inverted parabola and the total energy $E$ is a horizontal line; $U$ and $K$ cross at $E/2$.

(c) $E = \tfrac12 \times 100 \times 0.1^2 = 0.500$ J. At $x = 0$ all of it is kinetic, so $v_{\max} = \sqrt{2E/m} = 2.00$ m s$^{-1}$. At $x = 0.06$ m, $U = 0.180$ J, $K = 0.320$ J and $v = \sqrt{2K/m} = 1.60$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Work of the spring from A to x gives K; add U.

marking_scheme.step: Work by the spring from A to x is ½k(A² − x²) = ½mv²
U parabola, K inverted parabola, E horizontal line
E = 0.500 J and v(max) = 2.00 m s⁻¹
At x = 0.06 m: v = 1.60 m s⁻¹

questions.stem_md: (a) A constant force F acts on a body along its direction of motion with velocity v. Derive the expression for the power delivered by the force. [2] (b) A car of mass 1200 kg climbs a straight road that rises 1 m for every 20 m travelled along it (so sin θ = 1/20), at a steady 20 m s⁻¹. The resistance to motion (friction and air) is 500 N. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find the driving force and the power of the engine. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In a small time $dt$ the body moves $dS$ along the force, so the work done is $dW = F\,dS$. The power is $P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = F\dfrac{dS}{dt} = Fv$.

(b) At a steady speed the driving force balances the resistance plus the component of the weight down the slope. The component of the weight along the slope is $mg\sin\theta = 1200 \times 9.8 \times \tfrac{1}{20} = 588.0$ N. The driving force is $F = 500 + 588.0 = 1088$ N, and the power is $P = Fv = 1088 \times 20 = 21760$ W, or 21.8 kW.

questions.solution_md: Divide dW = F dS by dt; at steady speed the forces balance.

marking_scheme.step: dW = F dS in a small time dt
Weight component along the slope = 588.0 N

questions.stem_md: A 4.0 kg block, initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface, is pushed along a straight line by a force F that is 8.0 N from S = 0 to S = 3.0 m and then falls uniformly to zero at S = 7.0 m. (a) Sketch the force–displacement graph in words and find the work done by the force over the 7.0 m. [3] (b) Use the work–energy theorem to find the speed of the block at S = 7.0 m. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The graph is a horizontal line at 8.0 N up to 3.0 m, followed by a straight line falling to zero at 7.0 m. The work is the area under it. The rectangle has area $8.0 \times 3.0 = 24.0$ J and the triangle has area $\tfrac12 \times 4.0 \times 8.0 = 16.0$ J, so the total work is $40.0$ J.

(b) The surface is smooth, so this is the net work, and by the work–energy theorem it equals the gain in kinetic energy from rest: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = 40.0$ J. Hence $v = \sqrt{2 \times 40.0 / 4.0} = 4.472$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.solution_md: Rectangle plus triangle; then the theorem from rest.

marking_scheme.step: Graph: constant force, then a straight fall to zero
Net work = gain in kinetic energy from rest
